'''''Abies koreana''''' ({{langx|ko|구상나무}}, ''Gusang namu''), the '''Korean fir''', is a species of [[fir]] native to the higher [[mountain]]s of [[South Korea]], including [[Jeju Island]]. It grows at altitudes of {{convert|1,000|–|1,900|m}} in [[temperate rainforest]] with high rainfall and cool, [[Humidity|humid]] summers, and heavy winter snowfall.

== Description ==
It is a small to medium-sized [[evergreen]] [[Pinophyta|coniferous tree]] growing to {{convert|10|–|18|m|abbr=on}} tall with a trunk diameter of up to {{convert|0.7|m|abbr=on}}, smaller and sometimes [[shrub]]by at the [[tree line]]. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is smooth with [[resin]] blisters and grey-brown in colour. The [[leaves]] are needle-like, flattened, {{convert|1|–|2|cm|1}} long and {{convert|2|–|2.5|mm|2}} wide by {{convert|0.5|mm|2|abbr=on}} thick, glossy dark green above, and with two broad, vividly white bands of [[stomata]] below, and slightly notched at the tip. The leaf arrangement is spiral on the shoot, but with each leaf variably twisted at the base so they lie mostly either side of and above the shoot, with fewer below the shoot. The shoots are green-grey at first, maturing pinkish-grey, with scattered fine pubescence. The [[conifer cone|cones]] are {{convert|4|–|7|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.5|–|2|cm|1|abbr=on}} broad, dark purple-blue before maturity; the scale [[bract]]s are long, green or yellow, and emerge between the scales in the closed cone. The winged [[seed]]s are released when the cones disintegrate at maturity about 5–6 months after pollination.

== Cultivation ==
Korean fir is a very popular [[ornamental plant]] in parks and gardens in temperate climates, grown for its foliage but also for the abundant cone production even on young trees only {{convert|1|–|2|m|abbr=on}} tall. The following have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:
* ''A. koreana''<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/44/i-Abies-koreana-i/Details |title=''A. koreana'' |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=20 December 2017 |archive-date=27 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527111923/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/44/i-abies-koreana-i/details |url-status=live}}</ref> (≥ 12 m)
* ''A. koreana'' "Cis"<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/108732/Abies-koreana-Cis/Details |title=''A. koreana'' "Cis" |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=20 December 2017 |archive-date=27 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527114338/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/108732/abies-koreana-cis/details |url-status=live}}</ref> (0.5–1 m)
* ''A. koreana'' "Kohout's Ice Breaker"<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/314382/Abies-koreana-Kohout-s-Ice-Breaker-(PBR)/Details |title=''A. koreana'' "Kohout's Ice Breaker" |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=20 December 2017 |archive-date=27 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527115153/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/314382/abies-koreana-kohout-s-ice-breaker-(pbr)/details |url-status=live}}</ref> (0.5–1 m)
* ''A. koreana'' "Silberlocke"<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/73538/i-Abies-koreana-i-Silberlocke/Details |title=''A. koreana'' "Silberlocke" |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=20 December 2017 |archive-date=27 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527120316/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/73538/i-abies-koreana-i-silberlocke/details |url-status=live}}</ref> (2.5–4 m)

== Habitat ==
Biggest group of wild Korean fir grows in [[Hallasan]] Mountain in [[Jeju Island]], South Korea.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Yoon |first1=Hanna |title=Climate troubles loom for South Korea's "Christmas Tree Island" |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/climate-troubles-loom-south-korea-christmas-tree-island |access-date=26 December 2023 |work=National Geographic |date=2020-12-24 |archive-date=2024-05-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527120317/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/climate-troubles-loom-south-korea-christmas-tree-island |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Use ==
Korean fir is also used as a Christmas tree.<ref>{{cite news |author=Kwon Mee-yoo |title=Korean Fir Popular as Christmas Tree |url=https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/southkorea/20091224/korean-fir-popular-as-christmas-tree|access-date=26 December 2023 |work=The Korea Times |date=2009-12-24 |archive-date=2024-05-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527120930/https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/www/nation/2023/12/113_57895.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/choosing_the_right_christmas_tree |title=Real Christmas trees: Which one is right for you? |work=Michigan State University Extension |date= 2023-11-06 |access-date= 2023-12-26 |archive-date=2024-05-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240527121442/https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/choosing_the_right_christmas_tree |url-status=live}}</ref>
